title: The Weight of a Stone
logline: In a gem-cutting town, a stone is turned once under a lamp, and in less than a second a cutter says what it is worth, a judgement that took a lifetime to become instant.
human_question: What has to happen, in an instant, for someone to just know what they are looking at?

premise.story: A gem sorter or cutter examines rough and cut stones through a working day: tilting them to the light, judging colour, deciding what to buy, reject, or how to cut.
premise.place: A gem-trading room or small cutter's workshop in a mining district.
premise.experience: The viewer watches a judgement that looks instantaneous and comes to see how many small steps, arriving, being taken in, checked, settled, and finally acted on, are folded into that one glance.

concept_links.why: The source's full seventeen-moment process for a very great object, adverting, seeing, receiving, examining, determining, a burst of full engagement, then a brief holding, describes, at the level of doctrine, exactly the kind of instant, total judgement a practised eye makes over a stone; the series reads the concluding burst as where a response is made, though the source itself never calls this stage choice [C041-P:L46; C041-M:L7].

The source insists the eye meets only colour, not a ruby or a flaw; recognition is added from everything seen before. A gem cutter's snap judgement is built on exactly this gap between raw colour and trained naming.

Matter's own brief lifespan, seventeen mind-moments, is the source's account of why a full judgement has to happen fast or not at all, a useful, if technical, frame for why a trained eye works in an instant.

what_camera_could_observe: A stone tilted under a lamp, turned in the fingers
The moment a face changes as a verdict forms
A second look, or a colleague's differing opinion
Bargaining, rejection or a sale following the verdict
Cutting, grinding or polishing once a decision is made
what_must_be_real: The trade's real money, risk and secrecy; no staged verdicts for the camera; the cutter's own account of what a first look tells them versus what only a second look does.

possible_arc.opening: A stone changes hands; work for the day begins.
possible_arc.turn: A stone tests the cutter's judgement, an unusual colour, a hidden flaw, a disagreement with a buyer.
possible_arc.ending_open: The stone is bought, rejected, or cut; the outcome is whatever the trade actually decides.

position_hint: opening candidate: a real, demanding craft with a strong physical object, a gemstone, that could plausibly be where Object 5 is acquired, if a real moment allows.

requirements: An active gem-cutting or gem-trading workshop willing to allow filming
Consent covering security and trade confidentiality around valuable stones
Good close-up light and stable access for macro camera work

suggestions.name: Ratnapura gem-mining district
suggestions.why: Sri Lanka's best-known centre for gem mining, trading and cutting.
suggestions.access_notes: Security and confidentiality around stones will need careful negotiation.
suggestions.verify: A specific workshop, trader or cutter willing to be filmed is unconfirmed.

risks: The gem trade involves real money and security concerns that could limit access
Glamorising the trade without its labour and mining realities
Implying trade secrets or valuations on camera that could put someone at risk
drop_if: No trader or cutter will allow filming of real transactions
Security concerns make filming valuable stones impossible
The work cannot be shown without exposing confidential pricing or sourcing

connections.note: Both watch a trained eye separate raw colour from a name and a value, one with stones and one with flowers.
